item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to do what no Major League Baseball team has done in the last quarter-century and win three consecutive championships.
Despite all the talent on the roster, each name on the 26-man roster come postseason will have more importance than the next. Even someone like Miguel Rojas — who was hitless for a calendar month heading into the World Series — can come up big in perhaps the biggest moment in the history of the sport.
All of this not only boils down to how the two-time defending champions will perform, but who manager Dave Roberts names on the final rendition of the postseason rosters. As entertaining as the impending decision will be for onlookers of the baseball world, the skipper knows the importance of his roster choice as well as anyone.
Josue De Paula and Dalton Rushing appear to be fighting for the same thing come October, but De Paula is still a raw product and Rushing is still on the injured list with elbow discomfort.
“It’s going to be a good debate,” manager Dave Roberts said on Tuesday.
De Paula, the 21-year-old rookie from Brooklyn, NY, put up undeniable numbers in Double-A this season, leading to the outfielder's promotion before registering a single Triple-A at-bat. In his first 11 games in the big leagues, he's hitting .323/.500/.581 with a 1.081 OPS.
Rushing, on the other hand, has plenty more big league experience than De Paula since his promotion last May. Before his first IL stint, Rushing was hitting .253 with an OPS of .809 this season.
The reason for his stint on the shelf was due to a slight tear in his ulnar collateral ligament. After he returned for just four hitless games, he once again hit the injured list, but this time, MRIs gave reason to believe that the flexor tendon was the real issue, something that could potentially be addressed without surgery and assisted through platelet-rich plasma injections.
For either player, this will be an uphill battle. Roberts admitted that for Rushing specifically, it may be just a steeper incline.
“Hitting off the bench is very difficult and so you're just trying to figure out who gives us the best chance," Roberts said. “To be quite frank, it’s going to be tougher for Dalton given the time that he’s missed, and to kind of think that you have three games to get back in the playoff form, which is tough to do. It’s not a knock on him. He’s been great for us. but it’s still tough given that also you’re talking about the consistency of at-bats recently from Josue.
“We have to have those conversations and make a decision.”

Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles, California. The city of movie stars, names and big personalities. Oh yeah, and championships, with the two most recent going to the Dodgers. When you think about the Los Angeles Dodgers, the names that come to mind are Shohei, Tarik, Yoshinobu, and Mookie.
Not Max.
For one reason or another, Max Muncy has been an underappreciated player in this league for far too long. No, he’s not the typical profile to win an MVP; he doesn’t have the flair that matches the city, and maybe consistency just isn’t sexy.
But, remove Max Muncy from the Los Angeles Dodgers, and this season, along with their recent history, looks different.
Stats from prior to games on Sept. 20, 2026.
Muncy’s Importance in 2026
Although the Dodgers easily clinched another NL West title, I think it’s fair to say their season has not gone quite as planned. Crazy, right? When you have their amount of star power and top prospects, and you acquire Tarik Skubal at the deadline, anything less than the best record in baseball isn’t good enough.
Part of the reason why the Dodgers have not reached the extremely high expectations many placed on them is injuries. Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Roki Sasaki, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing, Edwin Díaz, Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and others all missed significant time on the IL.
Combine that IL time with Kyle Tucker’s ho-hum season and Mookie Betts not being quite the player he once was at the plate, and you can see why the Dodgers don’t quite look like an unstoppable force.
With so many injuries and inconsistencies in the lineup, the Dodgers needed Max Muncy more than ever. Even at 36 years old, Muncy is having an amazing season. He is slashing .254/.351/.500 with 29 home runs and a 132 wRC+, second on the team only to Ohtani’s 142 wRC+. Muncy’s 4.3 fWAR is first amongst Dodgers position players. Yes, that includes Ohtani.
He’s currently on pace to either match or surpass his career high of 4.5 fWAR from the 2021 season when he hit 36 home runs. If he doesn’t quite get to 4.5, 4.4 would tie his second-best season, which came in 2019 in the juiced-ball era. Yeah, I’d say Muncy’s doing pretty well.
After being such a consistent and healthy player throughout the beginning part of his career, Muncy missed parts of the last two seasons due to injury. Returning from injury to play over 140 games, and at this high of a level, goes to show what type of talent he is.
On the current roster, Muncy is one of three players with more than 20 home runs. Keep in mind, Ohtani also has more than 20, but he is on the IL. Muncy’s 29 home runs place him in the top 20 in all of baseball. We still saw his power in his injury-riddled seasons in 2024 and 2025, but seeing it return to this level has been a massive boost for the Dodgers.
Kyle Tucker was seen as a middle-of-the-order bat who could push Muncy down a spot, but as it has turned out, Muncy is more important than ever. Sure, this team would still have topped 90 wins without Muncy, but the lineup would feel much different. The hole created at third base would be filled by Miguel Rojas or Enrique Hernández, which is far from ideal. The drop-off from Muncy to whoever the replacement was would have been massive.
As you look ahead to the postseason, there are still questions around the Dodgers’ lineup. Pages recently returned from the IL, and Ohtani will soon, giving the Dodgers a much-needed boost. Pages adds another righty bat into the lineup and allows Tommy Edman to move back to the infield. Ohtani fills DH, which is currently held down by rookie Josue De Paula.
Muncy adds another veteran back with postseason experience. A .817 OPS and 16 career postseason home runs give the Dodgers another threat once the weather cools and the games become more important.
Yes, Muncy has been crucial to the Dodgers’ success this season. But you could really say that about his entire career.
Muncy’s Consistent Excellence
Let’s start back at the beginning. Max Muncy started with the Oakland Athletics before being released in 2017 and signing a minor league contract with the Dodgers. He debuted in LA in 2018, immediately finding success, slashing .263/.391/.582 with 35 home runs. From an Oakland castoff to hitting 35 home runs a year later was impressive, but it was just the beginning.
Muncy followed in 2019, repeating his 35-home run season, a mark he has posted four times since joining the Dodgers. Power has been an important part of his game, and so has consistency. From 2018 through 2023, Muncy logged at least 135 games each year, excluding the COVID season.
Of those six seasons, three were at 130 wRC+ or better, and five were over 100. Really, the only subpar season of his career came in 2020, when he had a 98 wRC+ and 12 home runs in 58 games.
His 2024 and 2025 shortened seasons were still, statistically, some of the best of his career. If we look at it just from a wRC+ standpoint, his 133 wRC+ in 2024 and 137 in 2025 rank in the top four in his career, while 2026 (132 wRC+) lands in the same discussion.
By now, you know what you’re getting with Muncy. Consistent power and one of the best walk rates in the league. His batting average isn’t going to wow anyone, and neither is his defense, although both are adequate in this day and age.
Max Muncy is one of the best Dodgers of all time, and you might not even realize it. His 238 career home runs rank fifth in Dodger history. He ranks seventh in walks, roughly 100 behind Jackie Robinson. Only 14 Dodgers have driven in more runs, and by the time Muncy hangs up the cleats, he could be near the top 10.
Year in and year out, Muncy gives the Dodgers exactly what they expect of him. Early in his career, he provided versatility around the diamond. If the team needed a second baseman, he’d play there. When they needed a first baseman in 2021, Muncy was the answer. Now, he’s settled into third base.
Three All-Star appearances and three World Series rings. I’d argue that he deserves more recognition. Not too bad for a guy that they got for next to nothing.
Final Thoughts
I know that the Dodgers have the type of star power that drives jersey sales. Who wouldn’t want to wear an Ohtani jersey? He’s the best player to ever play the game.
However, I wish we would see more Muncy jerseys at Dodger Stadium. In some ways, this might be a “you don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone” situation. Luckily, I think Muncy still has several more productive seasons left. He’s not showing signs of slowing down.
If you placed Max Muncy into a number of other cities, he would be their star. I guess it’s easy to get lost in Hollywood, which has over 2,800 of them.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Miguel Rojas has done something no other Dodger has done before.
Rojas was named the winner of the 21st annual Roy Campanella Award, the third year in a row that he’s taken the honor.
No other Dodger has won the award, which the team said is “is given to the Dodger player who best exemplifies the spirit and leadership of the late Hall of Fame catcher,” three straight years, though Justin Turner did win three awards in 2017, 2019 and 2020.
He’ll be honored before Thursday’s game by Campanella’s daughter, Joni Campanella Roan, and his granddaughter, Akua Campanella.
Why was Miguel Rojas honored with the Campanella award?
Rojas won the award through a vote by uniformed Dodgers personnel, and it makes sense given his “rock solid” performance this season.
Not only is he hitting .271 with four homers and 22 RBIs in 103 games, but he also has started at second base, shortstop and third base, racking up a .995 fielding percentage.
He also, of course, hit the game-tying home run in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series, forever stitching his name in Dodgers lore, though his on-field performance is far from all he brings to the team.
“Rojas’ excellent leadership in the clubhouse is by now common knowledge among baseball fans,” the team said in a news release. “The last four years, he’s instituted players-only, series-victory celebratory toasts in the locker room when the Dodgers take a series or record a sweep. Rojas will kick off the toasts with a few words and then throw it over to the ‘player of the game.’ He’s also famous for his mentorship of players both young and old, including Mookie Betts, Alex Freeland and Hyeseong Kim.”
What’s next for Miguel Rojas?
Rojas is expected to retire after this season, and “next year he is expected to transition into a front office job with a focus on player development,” the team said.
In the meantime, he’s soaking up what’s likely his final few weeks as an MLB player.
“I never take it for granted,” Rojas told Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez. “I feel like every opportunity we have to take this field is really special, especially after what happened the last couple of years, not just to me but to the organization and the city.”

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Veteran infielder Miguel Rojas was voted by his Dodgers teammates and coaching staff as the 2026 winner of the Roy Campanella Award, given annually to the Dodgers player who best embodies the leadership and spirit of the Hall of Fame catcher. Rojas also won the award in 2024 and 2025, making him the first player to win the Campanella Award in three straight seasons.
In the 21-year history of the award, Justin Turner is the only other player to win the Campanella Award three times, taking the honor in 2017, 2019, and 2020. Clayton Kershaw (2013-14) and Chase Utley (2016, 2018) are the only other Dodgers to win the award twice.
The 37-year-old Rojas was the first Dodgers player to speak ahead of the clubhouse celebration last Thursday in Cincinnati when the Dodgers clinched the National League West.
The longtime shortstop Rojas has started games at second base, shortstop, and third base this season, and even played three innings at first base. He's hitting .271/.311/.399 with a 93 wRC+ in his 101 games and 243 plate appearances, including a robust .297/.340/.476 with a 122 wRC+ against left-handed pitchers.
The Dodgers traded for Rojas prior to the 2023 season, and he has mentored young players and filled in all over the infield for the last four seasons. Rojas cemented his place in Dodgers lore with his game-tying home run in the ninth inning of Game 7 of the 2025 World Series at Toronto.
Rojas signed a one-year, $5.5 million contract in December to return for his 13th and final season, and plans to join the Dodgers front office afterward, with a focus on player development. Rojas has long stated his desire to get into coaching once his playing days are over.
"Nobody when I came to this organization asked me, 'Hey we want you to be a leader' or 'We want you to be a mentor.' It's just who I want to be and who I want to be for the future," Rojas told True Blue LA in 2024. "After my career is over, I'm trying to stay on the field, to stay coaching, and I want to be a part of an organization that wants to win."
Rojas will receive his 2026 Roy Campanella Award before Thursday night's series finale against the Padres, with Campanella's daughter, Joni Campanella Roan, and his granddaughter, Akua Campanella presenting Rojas with the award on the field at Dodger Stadium.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES – The Los Angeles Dodgers announced today that infielder Miguel Rojas was named the winner of the 21st annual Roy Campanella Award, which is given to the Dodger player who best exemplifies the spirit and leadership of the late Hall of Fame catcher. The award, which was voted upon by Dodger uniformed personnel, will be presented to Rojas by Campanella’s daughter, Joni Campanella Roan, and his granddaughter, Akua Campanella, during pregame ceremonies on Thursday night.
Rojas, 37, becomes the second player to win three Campanella awards, joining Justin Turner (2017, 2019-20) and he’s the very first to win three in a row. He’s one of four players to take home the honor multiple times, along with Clayton Kershaw (2013-14), Turner and Chase Utley (2016, 2018). Rojas also becomes the second oldest player to win the award, after Utley (37, 39).
Rafael Furcal received the inaugural Roy Campanella Award in 2006 and since then the honor has been awarded to Russell Martin (2007), James Loney (2008), Juan Pierre (2009), Jamey Carroll (2010), Matt Kemp (2011), A.J. Ellis (2012), Kershaw (2013-14), Zack Greinke (2015), Utley (2016, 2018), Turner (2017, 2019-20), Chris Taylor (2021), Freddie Freeman (2022), Jason Heyward (2023) and Rojas (2024-26).
Rojas has been rock solid at the plate in 2026, hitting .271 with four homers and 22 RBI in 103 games, while batting .297 (43-for-145) vs. left-handed pitching and .287 at UNIQLO Field at Dodger Stadium. Defensively, he’s been as steady as ever, starting 36 games at second base (135 chances without an error), 17 at shortstop and three at third while making just one error on the season, good for a .995 fielding percentage.
In 2025, the Dodgers brought the native of Venezuela back for another season, a decision that proved pivotal this season as made starts at second base (43), third base (20) and shortstop (10), before delivering one of the biggest home runs in World Series history. In the bottom of the ninth of Game 7 vs. the Blue Jays in Toronto, his one-out solo homer off Jeff Hoffmann tied the game at 4-4, allowing Los Angeles to comeback and win its second straight World Series with a 5-4 win in extra innings.
Rojas returned to the Dodgers in 2023 and signed a two-year deal, coming back to the organization where he made his Major League debut on June 8, 2014 and as the starting third baseman, helped preserve Clayton Kershaw’s no-hitter on June 18, 2014 with a stellar play. After hitting .236 in 2023, Rojas rebounded in a big way in 2024, hitting .283 in 103 games and playing his usual Gold Glove defense all over the diamond. Rojas also provided invaluable leadership to the club last year as he played on a World Series winner for the first time that year.
Rojas’ excellent leadership in the clubhouse is by now common knowledge among baseball fans. The last four years, he’s instituted players-only, series-victory celebratory toasts in the locker room when the Dodgers take a series or record a sweep. Rojas will kick off the toasts with a few words and then throw it over to the “player of the game.” He’s also famous for his mentorship of players both young and old, including Mookie Betts, Alex Freeland and Hyeseong Kim.
The slick-fielding veteran has mentioned that 2026 might be his final Major League season and next year he is expected to transition into a front office job with a focus on player development.
After the club won the National League West last week, Rojas said of his teammates: “This is family to me. These guys kept me positive and kept me going every single day. I can’t thank the guys enough for what they have done for me the last four years. I’m so excited for the opportunity to three-peat with this team.”
Campanella was a three-time National League Most Valuable Player (1951, 1953 and 1955), eight-time All-Star and a member of the 1955 World Championship team. He played in five World Series and his 142 RBI in 1953 set a franchise record, since surpassed by Tommy Davis (153 in 1962). In 1,215 career games during a 10-year career, all with the Dodgers, he batted .276 with 242 home runs and 856 RBI.
He began his career in the Negro Leagues, establishing himself as one of the top catchers in the league before joining the Dodger organization in 1946. Campanella played for Class B Nashua of the New England League, making that club the first integrated affiliated baseball team in the United States.
On Jan. 29, 1958, just as the Dodgers were making final preparations for their move to Los Angeles, Campanella was involved in a tragic car accident that paralyzed him from the neck down, marking the end of his playing career. On May 7, 1959, a Major League record-setting 93,103 fans filled the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on “Roy Campanella Night” for an exhibition game between the Dodgers and Yankees.
He was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1969 and was among the first three Dodgers to have their uniform numbers retired alongside Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax. Campanella remained active in the Dodgers’ Community Relations Department until his death on June 26, 1993, at the age of 71.
The Los Angeles Dodgers franchise, with nine World Series championships and 26 National League pennants since its beginnings in Brooklyn in 1890, is committed to a tradition of pride and excellence. The Dodgers, baseball’s 2024 and 2025 back-to-back World Champions, are the reigning Sports Business Journal Sports Team of the Year, have been recognized as ESPN’s Sports Humanitarian Team of the Year and are dedicated to supporting a culture of winning baseball, providing a first-class, fan-friendly experience, and building a strong partnership with the community. With the highest cumulative fan attendance in Major League Baseball history and a record of breaking barriers, the Dodgers are one of the most cherished sports franchises in the world. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Miguel Rojas is nearing the end of what’s widely expected to be his final regular season as an MLB player, but he’s got a very good reason not to let up off the gas pedal.
Rojas is a native of Venezuela, but he is applying for his United States citizenship, reports Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register.
That application requires him to take the citizenship test, and that’s where things can get dicey with baseball’s postseason schedule.
Rojas is set to take that test on Oct. 1, which is the third day of the three-game wild card series.
If the Dodgers were to have to play that round of the playoffs, it “would complicate his travel” to take the exam, Plunkett wrote on social media.
How likely are the Dodgers to get a bye for the wild card round?
Fortunately for Rojas — and the Dodgers as a whole — they seem to have a good hold on the second seed in the National League, which includes a bye for the wild card round.
As of Tuesday morning, the Dodgers have a four game lead over the third-place Atlanta Braves, and with only six regular season games remaining for each team, the Braves are running out of time to make up ground.
As long as the Dodgers can hold off the Braves, Rojas will be available to take his citizenship test, and the injury-plagued Dodgers will also get a few extra days to heal up ahead of a grueling October.
A last dance for Miguel Rojas
Aside from getting his American citizenship, Rojas can also use that time off to soak up his last season as an MLB player.
The hero of the 2025 World Series doesn’t really have anything left to prove, but he told Dodgers Nation’s Noel Sanchez that he’s trying to make the most of his playing time.
“I never take it for granted,” he said. “I feel like every opportunity we have to take this field is really special especially after what happened the last couple of years, not just to me but to the organization and the city.”
It is possible, though, that Rojas isn’t quite done.
He has flirted with the idea of coming back for another season, something contingent on the Dodgers three-peating, but he notes that’s only his desire.
Even if he changed his mind and wanted to come back, the team could decide to move on.
“I don’t really know when it’s going to be my last time stepping out to home plate and hearing the crowd cheer for me and support me, and that’s the reason why I’m getting a little bit emotional,” he said. “Even though I said I might come back and play if we win the World Series, there’s no guarantee.”
But that’s a worry for later.
For now, Rojas is still focused on the three-peat, and he’s soaking up every second.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers on Tuesday got a few regulars back as reinforcements heading into the final week of the regular season and into October, activating center fielder Andy Pages and pitcher Roki Sasaki off the injured list.
Pages missed 27 games after getting hit by a fastball on his left hand on August 21. Sasaki left his start in Atlanta five days later with a blister on his right middle finger.
Emmet Sheehan and catcher Eliezer Alfonzo were optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City on Monday.
Pages was an All-Star starter this season, and when he got hurt was tied with Yoshinobu Yamamoto for second-highest FanGraphs WAR (3.9) on the team, behind only Shohei Ohtani. By Baseball Reference WAR, Pages is still third on the team now at 5.4, trailing only Ohtani and Yamamoto. That’ll happen with a .272/.338/.458 batting line with a 118 wRC+ combined with plus-defense in center field.
Before getting hit by an errant fastball on August 21, Pages started 125 of the Dodgers’ 129 games, and led the team in plate appearances (550) at the time. Pages and Ohtani are still tied for the Dodgers’ lead with 80 runs batted in. With Pages out, Alek Thomas was first called up to start six games in center field, followed by Tommy Edman starting 17 games, plus three starts by Alex Call and one by Kiké Hernández.
With Edman moving to the outfield and once Thomas was optioned, Miguel Rojas (10) and Alex Freeland (eight) have covered all but one of the starts at second base in September.
Sasaki struggled earlier in the season, but improved as the season progressed. He has a streak of six straight starts with no more than two runs allowed until his blister start in Atlanta. On the season, Sasaki has a 4.46 ERA and 4.42 xERA, but since July 8 he’s down to a 3.25 ERA and 3.76 xERA in eight starts.
With Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and Tyler Glasnow set for the postseason rotation, the Dodgers will see over the next two weeks if Blake Snell will be hampered by his left groin discomfort, and will have Sheehan at the ready. That allows them to use Sasaki in relief, as they did last postseason out of necessity.
“I could see multiples [innings], but it’s not going to be bulk as in four or five innings,” manager Dave Roberts said on Sunday.
Last season was a different situation for Sasaki, who struggled mightily as a starter and spend four months on the injured list before returning in the final week of the regular season. There was no room in the rotation, so he pitched in relief in the postseason. He wasn’t dominant — only six strikeouts among his 43 batters faced, with five walks — but he was effective, allowing only one run over nine appearances and 10 2/3 innings, the highlight his perfect three innings of relief in the Dodgers’ NLDS Game 4 clincher over the Philadelphia Phillies.
Sasaki saved three games last postseason. Roberts said Sasaki probably wouldn’t get an opportunity in a save situation right away this week, but it could progress to that by the postseason.
“I trust Roki in any situation. I would say probably starting a clean inning,” Roberts said. “He’s done it, he’s really good. He’s a neutral pitcher, high-octane stuff. And you really just need four starters. So we’re in a good spot there, for now.”
Sheehan has been fantastic of late, allowing only one run in three starts for the Dodgers over the previous two weeks, with 24 strikeouts in 17 innings. The plan for Sheehan is to start on Saturday for Oklahoma City should the Comets advance to the Triple-A championship game.
Alfonzo was back with the Dodgers since September 6 when Dalton Rushing was placed on the injured list with elbow soreness. In the 14 games since, Alfonzo played only once, pinch-hitting as the designated hitter at the end of a 14-1 blowout of the Cincinnati Reds. He struck out.
Alfonzo made his major league debut against the Padres on July 5, and started nine games behind the plate. He had five hits in 28 at-bats with three doubles and four runs batted in.
